title: We're a metal band making a maths game for kids. Got our drummer walking this week - and hit a palette wall.
author: Big_Tie_5160
selftext:
We're Circulo Numerico, a folk metal band from Spain, and we also make a free browser game for kids: a maths adventure where the five of us show up as characters. Two are already playable in the bonus stage. This week we tried to add Morgan, our drummer.

  
Our normal pipeline has no AI in it. We have detailed reference art for each band member and we shrink the big originals straight down to about 172 px tall. That lands around 4,200 to 6,000 unique colours per sprite, which is the look we want: 16-bit SNES / Mega Drive rather than chunky 8-bit.

  
What we tried: [spritesheets.ai](http://spritesheets.ai), fed one clean reference frame of Morgan, asked for a side-view walk cycle, using their reference style lock option so it wouldn't restyle him.

  
What worked, and it genuinely surprised me:

\- Character consistency across all 61 output frames. The welding goggles on his forehead, the hair, the arm tattoos, the studded wristbands, the belt chain, none of it drifts. That is normally where these tools fall apart.

\- Alpha came back binary clean. 0.000 percent semi-transparent pixels, no halo. Better than the cutout we had made ourselves.

\- Character height stayed within 276 to 287 px across all frames, so no vertical bobbing to fix.

  
What didn't work: the palette. Measured at native size with no resampling, 254 unique colours per frame. Our existing in-game characters sit at 4,268 and 5,962. That is about 17x flatter, on a bigger canvas. 254 sitting just under 256 makes me think something in the chain quantises to an 8-bit palette. Side by side with the character we already ship, it reads muddy.

  
Where we landed: I found the cycle period by comparing silhouettes (12 frames), took every 3rd to get 4, and normalised them to a uniform 98x172 window aligned on a common foot line and torso centre. Uniform window matters. Cropping each frame to its own bbox gave us 12 px of lateral jitter last time and the character looked like he was vibrating. Morgan now walks in the bonus stage. Provisionally. He is just visibly duller than the guy standing next to him.

  
This was their Basic tier, which they themselves flag as the weakest for fine detail and cross-frame consistency, so it is not a verdict on the tool's ceiling. Standard is the next test.

  
Disclosure: they run a free-credits programme for posting about them and we are in it. The numbers are measured and the mixed verdict is ours.

comments.author: fitm3
comments.body:
one have an AI build you a complete sprite software (which it can do quite nicely)

Two if you can muster it get the AI to drive the best video models to make the sprite actions. I do comfy ui local make the character make a character sheet and feed my character into minimal h3 and it makes great animated sprites.  The sprite software the ai makes lets me fine tune it. 

My local only approach has limits for sure but has made some amazing things. 

If you want to have things worked out like a sprite being visually duller just have the AI do a critique and adjustments too it can balance things nicely. Take a short prompt of what you want and ask an ai to make a long prompt of doing it spinning up multiple agents and reviewing it .

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: Lower the frame rate so you have less touching up to do. Also why not use a proper power of 4 for sprite sizes? Think 1024 or 256 instead of 172.
